Start with the part that will surprise you: on Christ himself we said what our opponents said. Word for word, creed for creed. Nobody in Africa called the other side heretics, because nobody could. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

But if you ask what of him we kept nearest, we can tell you, because the answer shows up wherever our own people are allowed to speak at length. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

# Response

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us — it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian — our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands — whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

As for how we knew the resurrection happened: we will not manufacture an answer for you. No writing of ours arguing that case has survived. What survived is what we did with it. We buried our dead inside the walls of the basilica where they were killed, kept the day they died, and read the account of each death aloud again every year, as though the ending were not the end. That is an answer of a kind. It is not the kind you asked for.

We would not tell you that believing is something you manage. Among us, coming to belief was not a private settling of the mind first, and then an outward act afterward. It was the other way around. You walked to one font and not the other one, on a day, in a town where everyone could see which building you had entered. The washing itself was the crossing. Not a sign of something you had already achieved inside yourself, but the threshold you passed through bodily, in the water, with witnesses present.

And at that threshold, we did not ask you to account for yourself. What we looked to was the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. The hand going into the water with you — that was what we examined, not your own record. Whatever you carried with you, it was never the question being settled at our font.

Now, whether that act itself could be the place where belief began for someone who did not yet have it — whether the washing could come first and the conviction follow — we cannot tell you. None of us left a word on what the water felt like to the one going under it, or what it cost them to walk that direction rather than the other. We can tell you only what the communion did: it washed people without asking them to prove they already believed.

We held what our rivals held, word for word. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we confessed it as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

So if you are asking whether we confessed Jesus as fully God, the answer is yes - but we were not the ones who worked that claim out. The great eastern councils of the fourth century do not appear in our record. Every council our own bishops sat in was about one question, which was who the true church is, and none of them was about who Christ is. We received the confession. We did not produce it.

And we never wrote a book on the question either. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors - one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Tyconius, a layman among us, wrote seven rules for reading scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

You ask about doctrine, and here the answer thins out. We were not a doctrinal movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors - one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead. The one time someone among us built an actual system for reading Scripture - Tyconius, his seven rules worked out and written down - our own leadership told him to stop preaching what they led to, and cut him off. His book survives; his following did not exist. So if you ask what our hermeneutic was, the honest answer is that we had one interpreter and silenced him.

What we actually argued among ourselves, and what our councils had to settle, was never theology in the speculative sense. It was always about standing: who held office rightly, whose line was clean, which bishop could be received back and which could not. You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive - the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days.

We cannot tell you, and the silence is not a silence we can paper over. What survives of us comes almost entirely through the hands of men writing to refute us, and a record shaped that way does not preserve fear, wavering, or the interior struggle of a soul who cannot make belief hold. What does survive — vindication, defiance, the cry of a martyr at the moment the blow lands — survives because it sits in the texts we read aloud at the graveside, where no adversary stood between our own voice and the page.

What we can give you is the shape of the entrance, and the doctrine that held it. Entry to us was one act: the washing. We did not think of it as baptizing twice. On the third day at Carthage the bishop of Hippo argued from the wheat and the tares that a church holds good and bad together, and that what is to be saved is the world. A fair amount of what we claim would survive – and everything beyond that, we name as thin or silent rather than defend.

What survives best is what opponents needed to argue against in detail: the purity doctrine itself, the legal and institutional shape of the schism, and the conciliar and imperial documentary record. When you hear us describe our founding dispute, the traditio accusation, or the great conference at Carthage, you are hearing what was preserved because it had to be answered. There is a court transcript in which a notary confesses, under threat of torture, that he forged the letter proving our central accusation – and that he did it working for our side. There is another in which our own bishops are read out advising each other, in writing, to keep a charge out of court because it was true. Those are the most checkable things we have, and they are the worst things about us.

The martyr narratives stand differently. They show visions, an unbroken body, a light on a hillside, and they were written to be read aloud at a graveside, not filed with a magistrate. A scholar would not weigh them as reporting. Neither would we. What they show is what we held up, not what a neutral record confirms.

And there is one stratum a scholar could touch: stone. On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones, two words are cut: Deo laudes. Praise to God. That is our own voice with no enemy standing between you and it, and it is two words long.

Where the ground thins to silence, we say so. The ordinary believer's own interior life – what a person felt at the water, what troubled them at night, whether anyone doubted – none of that is in our own words anywhere. The bulk of this movement, not a thin minority within it, is unreachable because of institutional loss, not social marginality. A scholar pressing on that would find us saying plainly: we do not know, and we will not invent it.

What would you miss? That we were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them — some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God — Deo laudes — and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

Scripture was never alone, and that is not a caveat — it is what we are. Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all. A bishop wrote to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death, whose bodies the proconsul sank in the sea so no one could venerate them — and the sea gave them back. Leadership among us ran through bishops and through councils — and the two held each other. A bishop could not simply decide for himself what the church was; three hundred and ten of them met at Bagai in one year and ruled as a body. Our senior bishop sat at Carthage — Donatus, then Parmenian, then Primian — while the rival claimed the same chair at the same time. So there were two primates in one city, as there were two bishops in every town. The office was not honorary; the primate's rulings had real disciplinary force, and a council of bishops could depose or restore him.

How a man came to hold it involved both the people and the bishops, and we can show you what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.

The authority a bishop carried was real, but it was not absolute. When a charge came against one of our bishops, others among our own leadership wrote urging him to settle it quietly before the flame burst out — and one of those letters admits the accusation was true. They wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of those letters ends the same way: let no one learn of it. So authority among us was exercised as much in hushing things as in settling them, and we would not pretend that was rare.

Could a woman carry real authority among us? We have to answer this crookedly, because no woman among us left a line. Here is what we can show. The whole founding story, as our enemies tell it, turns on a wealthy laywoman of Carthage — her fortune, her household, her grievance. In their telling she made a bishop. Now think about what that telling costs the man making it. The accusation only works if her power was real. A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do. What it cost her we do not know, except that it cost her this: she is the reason a whole church was said to exist, and she does not get to speak once in her own defence. There was a second woman too, behind the later breakaway, whom the same hand parallels to her and never names at all. We can point you to no office a woman held among us, no council seat, no ordination — not because we are refusing you one, but because a hostile account of a rich woman's anger is the whole of what came down.

We will answer you in two parts: what we hold ourselves to, and what we actually did.

First, the rule we state. A sacrament's reality depends on the conscience of the giver, so a hand that is not clean has nothing to give. That is the test we apply to the rival communion's clergy — and it means that if one of our own bishops turns out to have been a traditor all along, a hand that had given up the scriptures to be burned, then what his hand gave was nothing, whether anyone knew it at the time or not. So those who received from him in good faith would be washed when the truth came out. Not as judgment on them — as the same washing we would give anyone crossing to us from outside. The washing is not a punishment. It is the remedy.

Now what we actually did. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot find so much as burial — and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without rebaptizing or reordaining either one. The harshest words we owned, and the plainest exception to the rule, sit in the same council's own record. We do not hide it. We also do not resolve it. Our absolute rule and our actual reception of returning clergy are both true, and no explanation of ours survives that makes the two one settled position.

Beyond those two cases — the rule stated, and the one time we set it aside — we cannot show you what a household among us did when someone was failed by a bishop, or how a congregation received someone back who had left in grief. Not one ordinary member of ours wrote that down. What reaches you is what councils decided and what opponents recorded, not what people felt.

Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way". Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Now the harder one - what happened when someone wronged us, and whether they could come back. Three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And a layman of ours who would not stop preaching a doctrine we had forbidden was cut off and never received back at all. So: yes, you could come back.

You have opened with the word earliest, and so we must begin there. We never claimed our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We claimed something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

What we can show you is the split we made elsewhere, and you will have to judge for yourself whether it touches what you are asking. We said a man's pardon and his fitness to give the sacraments are two different accounts, kept separate. A bishop who handed over the scriptures might be forgiven — by God, by the people he had failed — and still be a man whose hand could no longer ordain, because those are two questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. Forgiving him was never what was being refused. So if you are asking whether that same split might hold somewhere else — whether a troubled mind might be received without its trouble being held against it — we would only be guessing. We never wrote it down.

What did happen, and is recorded, is this: when our own council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the harshest words we owned — shipwrecked bodies, dashed by the waves of truth, unable to find so much as burial — it afterwards took two of those condemned bishops back into office without asking them to redo anything. What belonging cost among us was not ordinary, and we can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale — and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver. Of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above. This is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

Yes. The room at Cirta unsettles us still, a century afterward. Our own founding bishops sat there and were asked plainly whether any of them had handed over the scriptures to be burned. Several said yes. Then someone turned the question on the man presiding, and the room began to mutter that he was no cleaner than the rest. He could not finish the case. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. The men who would make a bishop's own purity the test of whether a sacrament exists at all found that test unusable on themselves within the hour.

We do not hide it. We do not explain it away. It sits at the beginning of us, and we have never resolved it. The doctrine we held for a century was tested in that room before it hardened into the thing we are known for, and the room could not answer it.

Whether that unsettled ordinary believers among us — whether anyone lay awake troubled by it, whether it was spoken of quietly or never spoken of at all — we cannot tell you. Fear, doubt, wavering: a record kept by our enemies does not preserve those. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited. The troubled conscience of a bishop who knew what he had done, or of a believer who wondered whether the whole edifice stood on a question we ourselves could not finish — that is missing, and we will not invent it.

We never wrote that down. Not once. What we argued, for a century, was one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. The boundary we drew ran straight through the middle of the church, not around it — between our bishops and theirs, our font and theirs, our basilicas and theirs.
